articles.title: Repeated air traffic control failures leave us in worrying territory
articles.summary: The question is whether all of these incidents were isolated and unavoidable, or whether they point to something more systemic.
articles.body:
To have one air traffic control failure in a fortnight may be regarded as a misfortune, to have two looks like carelessness. The UK's air traffic services provider is coming in for a wave of criticism at the moment, so where is it all leading?

The incident at the National Air Traffic Services (Nats) main control centre in Swanwick earlier this month was extremely serious. It caused more than 2,000 flight cancellations over two days, affecting hundreds of thousands of passengers . Some were left sleeping on airport floors, others were stranded in foreign airports.

Monday's failure at the Prestwick centre, which looks after air traffic in Scotland, northern England and northern Ireland was not as dramatic. But according to the aviation analytics company Cirium, it still led to about 150 flights being cancelled and many other delays affecting tens of thousands of travellers.

The first failure this month was attributed to a previously undetected software flaw, which had an impact due to a very specific set of circumstances combining in a millisecond. Today's issue was blamed on a "connectivity issue" specific to the system used in Scotland. The two, Nats says, were unrelated.

But this is becoming worryingly familiar territory.

In August 2023, on a bank holiday weekend, a problem with a single aircraft's flight plan caused a key system at Swanwick to break down, leading to cancellations and delays that affected 700,000 passengers.

Two years later, a smaller "radar-related issue" disrupted air traffic for four hours, and led to the cancellation of 150 flights.

The question is whether all of these incidents were isolated and unavoidable, or whether they point to something more systemic.

Airlines criticise air traffic control as second glitch causes more disruption

UK flight delays continue after issue with air traffic control in Scotland is fixed

There is no question that the job Nats has to do is fiendishly complicated, looking after some of the busiest airspace in Europe - including the approaches to Heathrow and Gatwick - which means handling up to 8,000 flights a day.

Visiting the Swanwick centre, it's hard not to be impressed by the sheer scale of the place, where hundreds of staff sit behind an array of large radar screens, calmly making sense of what looks to the untrained eye like utter chaos. But these controllers need reliable equipment, and the concern is that they aren't getting it.

Steve Heapy, chief executive of Jet2 made the point: "It is simply not good enough for this critical national infrastructure to keep letting customers down."

Easyjet said the latest incident "calls into question the resilience of Nats' systems and demonstrates the need for firm actions to prevent these repeated failures."

A Nats spokesperson, apologising for the latest issue, said technology "can and sometimes does fail. Our job is minimising disruption where possible."

They continued: "What isn't acceptable is any incident where safety is compromised - this is always our first priority."

Sources say that behind the scenes, airlines are "furious" that disruption keeps on happening, and that they have to bear the costs of refunding passengers and looking after those who are affected by delays. There are deep concerns that not enough resources are being put into ensuring the air traffic control system has the resilience it needs.

Some have gone further. Ryanair, for example, has repeatedly called for the Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe to resign, or failing that for the Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander to remove him from his post.

But although Alexander has described the disruption in early September as "completely unacceptable", there seems little appetite to force through a change of leadership at Nats.

The government has asked the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) to carry out an independent review of the first incident from this month, which is expected to take six months to complete.

Action is unlikely before the CAA's report appears, and today's events do not appear to have changed that.

Meanwhile, Rolfe made it clear on Friday that he has no plans to resign. He emphasised that in systems of such complexity, obscure faults are extremely hard to prevent.

"We spent so much time making sure they work that anything that does happen of this nature is, by its very nature, going to be incredibly complicated and probably difficult to understand at the time," he said.

Nevertheless, it is clear that impatience with the Nats failures is growing, both among the airlines that pay for air traffic services and among passengers who bear the brunt when systems do not work as they should.

articles.title: Invitation for men to 'experience hot flushes' at Hull event
articles.summary: A MenoVest will allow people at an event in Hull to experience one of the symptoms of the menopause.
articles.body:
Partners of women going through the menopause are being invited to experience one of the symptoms at a forthcoming support event.

At the Menopaus'ull Support Network event in Hull next month, health group Over The Bloody Moon will be taking one of its MenoVests, allowing people to experience a hot flush – one of the symptoms of the menopause.

Sarah Weichardt, who co-manages the project, said: "We're particularly interested in getting men along to come and experience the MenoVest, just so that they can understand what women go through."

The event will be at Princes Quay shopping centre on 17 October, from 10:30 until 14:30 BST.

"It's not just a hot flush, it's what the hot flush brings with it," said Weichardt.

"So it could be panic, it could be anxiety. It's experiencing it all at the same time."

She said she hoped the vest would give people a "better understanding of what women are going through".

"The more people we can get to experience it, the better," she added.

The menopause describes the end of a woman's reproductive years, and often happens at about the age of 50.

The period leading up to this is called the perimenopause, which is when many women notice their periods becoming unpredictable.

Other symptoms can include mood shifts, difficulty sleeping, and discomfort during sex.

Weichardt said her organisation had a banner with nearly 40 symptoms on it.

Many women "don't necessarily know that they're going into the menopause or they're perimenopausal" until they see the banner – and then they sometimes have a "lightbulb moment", she said.

Once women have "accepted it and are happy" they are menopausal or peri-menopausal, they can seek the support they need, she added.

There is also a Menopaus'ull Support Network event in Beverley on 10 October between 10:30 and 13:30 BST at the Toll Gavel Church.

articles.title: California removed levees from a former dairy farm, turning it back into wetlands where 16,000 waterbirds were counted in one day
articles.summary: US News: A former dairy pasture in California underwent a major transformation after levees were removed to restore tidal wetlands at the Giacomini Wetlands. T.
articles.body: A former dairy pasture in California underwent a major transformation after levees were removed to restore tidal wetlands at the Giacomini Wetlands. The restoration allowed tidal waters to return, triggering rapid changes in vegetation and wildlife. Over the following years, salt and brackish marsh expanded, while native-dominated plant communities increased and non-native-dominated communities declined. The response was also visible in bird numbers. Waterbird numbers grew sharply in the initial years after restoration, reaching a record high of approximately 16,000 birds counted on a single day in December 2013. Ten-year monitoring found that the restored wetland had entered a more stable ecological condition.How did California’s former dairy pasture change after levee breachingThe vegetation changes continued during the years after restoration. The National Park Service reported that salt and brackish marsh communities had increased by 143 acres by 2018 compared with the 2003 pre-restoration mapping, rising from 9 per cent of the project area to 37 per cent. Native California cordgrass also expanded substantially, growing across 21 per cent of the project area compared with 0.02 per cent before restoration.The restoration also changed the balance between native- and non-native-dominated vegetation. According to the National Park Service, non-native-dominated and mixed-nativity communities declined from 327 acres in 2008 to 164 acres in 2018, while native-dominated communities increased from 80 acres to 257 acres over the same period. The agency said the site had developed greater diversity of plant communities, become more similar to native reference marshes and provided valuable habitat for wildlife.Waterbird numbers change after California marsh restorationAccording to a monitoring summary by Avocet Research Associates, published by the National Park Service, “Waterbird numbers grew sharply in the initial years following restoration”, with a record high of approximately 16,000 waterbirds counted on a single day in December 2013. The source also reported that numbers began tapering off in 2014 and 2015 and remained similar during monitoring in 2017 and 2018.Two surface-feeding duck species were particularly abundant after restoration. Green-winged teal and American wigeon together accounted for 43.3 per cent of all waterbirds present between September and February. The source said the reduced waterbird numbers at Giacomini might have reflected changes in regional migration patterns caused by other tidal wetland restoration projects in San Francisco Bay, while another possibility was that resources had been limited by the early abundance of waterfowl.How did Giacomini Wetlands change after restorationThe increase in birds was part of wider ecological changes recorded at Giacomini. However, the source said the rapid growth eventually gave way to a more stable ecological condition as newly created niches became occupied and abundant resources were depleted.By the period between Year 5 and Year 10, the Giacomini Wetlands had reached what the National Park Service described as a “dynamic equilibrium” condition. The agency said that while birds, native fish and benthic invertebrates appeared to have reached a sustainable status quo, less tangible indicators such as biogeochemical processes and nutrient cycles might still have been changing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Neath Port Talbot council leader quits after becoming 'heavily intoxicated' at conference
articles.summary: Steve Hunt apologised and blamed "personal" reasons for his behaviour and "banter".
articles.body:
A council leader who fell over while drunk after allegations he drank a "whole bottle of gin" and then threatened to "wipe out" the Welsh party Plaid Cymru has quit.

Steve Hunt, from Neath Port Talbot Council, said he "should have exercised better judgement" after becoming "intoxicated" at a Welsh Local Government Association conference.

Hunt said he was a strong supporter of the Welsh language, but admitted saying he wanted to "wipe out" Plaid Cymru politically as "banter".

Hunt will continue to serve as an independent councillor, but a council spokesperson said a new leader would be appointed on 14 October.

A source who attended the conference told the Local Democracy Reporting Service the independent councillor for the Crynant, Onllwyn and Seven Sisters ward was loudly bragging about drinking heavily.

Hunt said the comment about Plaid Cymru "should be understood in the context of political banter and disagreement at the end of a long evening, rather than as a threat or anything other than a political statement".

The councillor also said there were "personal circumstances" that contributed to his behaviour which were "relevant".

His role as council leader had carried a "significant level of pressure and responsibility", he said, and he saw the event as an opportunity to "switch off" from those pressures.

"Regrettably, I drank far beyond what was sensible," he said.

Hunt said it did not excuse his behaviour and that he apologised to the Plaid Cymru group leader the following morning.

Hunt has led the council's Independent and Plaid Cymru coalition since local elections took place in 2022.

It was the first time in Neath Port Talbot's history that the Labour Party lost control of the council.

Following his decision to step down, Hunt said he had done what he believed was in the "best interests" of the council and residents and communities that it represents.

"I will continue to serve as an Independent councillor and will continue to work for the residents and communities I represent," he said.

articles.title: Carney condemns Yom Kippur shooting outside Canadian synagogue
articles.summary: The Sunday night shooting left an officer in critical-but-stable condition and the suspect in life-threatening condition.
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and other politicians have condemned antisemitic violence after a shooting near a Jewish synagogue left a police officer critically injured.

The shooting took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, on Sunday night during Yom Kippur, the holiest night in the Jewish calendar.

Police have not provided a motive or said whether the synagogue was targeted, but said a suspect armed with a shotgun opened fire on a police officer stationed outside.

"Jewish people must be able to worship safely," Carney wrote on X. "To live free, open, proud Jewish lives."

The shooting occurred around 19:00 local time on Sunday night, Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) spokesperson Kristy Denette said on Monday. The officer returned fire and another officer discharged their firearm as well, Denette said.

Around 20 to 30 shots were fired, leaving the suspect in life-threatening condition and one officer in critical but stable condition, Denette said.

"It would have been quite, quite the scene indeed," she added.

Asked whether the incident was being considered a terrorist attack, Denette said that "common sense would say that probably was the case".

Echoing Carney's condemnation, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he is "disgusted" by the shooting and that members of the Jewish community "have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear".

Canadian opposition leader Pierre Poilievre wrote on social media that "this vile antisemitic violence in Canada must end" while urging Carney's government to "act now to protect our people".

Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks said the Belleville Police Service has increased patrols and will maintain a heightened presence around the city, including near places of worship.

The police service is still investigating the incident, as is the SIU, a watchdog that investigates officer-involved shootings.

Police in Toronto, which is about 116 miles (187km) away from Belleville, also said they were increasing patrols outside synagogues and places of worship out of an abundance of caution.

articles.title: Muhammad Ali’s 1915 Los Angeles mansion was bought for $2.5 million in 2001, restored while retaining its Tiffany stained glass, listed for nearly $17 million and finally sold for $8.5 million in 2024
articles.summary: US News: The former Los Angeles home of three-time world heavyweight boxing champion Muhammad Ali, a 1915 Italian Renaissance mansion in the gated Fremont Plac.
articles.body: The former Los Angeles home of three-time world heavyweight boxing champion Muhammad Ali, a 1915 Italian Renaissance mansion in the gated Fremont Place community, sold for $8.5 million (£6.7 million) in July 2024. The sale ended a long period on the market for the historic property. The house was first listed for almost $17 million ($16.995 million) in late 2022 before going through several price cuts and eventually being offered at auction.Historic estate in gated Fremont PlaceLocated at 55 Fremont Place near Hancock Park, the 11,545-square-foot estate sits on about 1.6 acres. Architect John C. Austin, who also designed Los Angeles City Hall and the Griffith Observatory, designed the home, which was built in 1915. Ali lived in the mansion during the late 1970s and 1980s with his third wife, Veronica, and their daughters, Laila and Hana. During his time there, the house welcomed many well-known guests, including world leaders, entertainers and sports stars. The estate has nine bedrooms and seven bathrooms in the main house. A separate guest house adds another bedroom and full bathroom. The grounds also include a heated swimming pool, spa, landscaped lawns, stone paths and a large outdoor patio for entertaining.Historic architecture and interior featuresDeveloper Michael R. Kaplan and his wife, Tari, bought the property in 2001 for about $2.5 million. They spent several years restoring the home, updating its modern systems while keeping many of its original architectural details. The preserved features include original Tiffany stained-glass windows, French Empire crystal chandeliers and carved wooden wall panels. The house also has marble and hardwood floors, several fireplaces, hand-carved mouldings and large bay windows. According to real estate listing records published by Zillow and Redfin, the mansion includes a glass-domed sunroom, a formal dining room with historic light fixtures, a main bedroom with two dressing rooms, a media room and a full cellar.Market history and final auction saleAfter the renovations were completed, the owners first listed the property for $16 million in August 2021. The listing was later withdrawn and returned to the market in November 2022 with a higher asking price of $16.995 million. According to The Real Deal, a Los Angeles real estate news publication, the price was lowered to $15 million in early 2023. When no buyer agreed to that price, the owners decided to put the property up for auction with no minimum price in May 2024 through Concierge Auctions. Property records maintained by Zillow show that the sale officially closed on July 18, 2024, for $8.5 million. That was about 50 per cent below the property's 2022 asking price.Legacy of the Fremont Place communityFremont Place is one of Los Angeles' oldest private gated communities. It was established in 1911 in the Mid-Wilshire area near Hancock Park. The neighborhood has 73 single-family homes, many designed by well-known 20th-century architects. Over the years, the community has been home to Hollywood stars, business leaders and civic officials. Redfin property records show that homes in the area continue to command high prices, with 55 Fremont Place among the community's largest properties. The July 2024 sale transferred ownership of the historic mansion for the first time in 23 years, bringing a new chapter to one of Hancock Park's best-known historic homes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: April Paul was found with her umbilical cord still attached in a phone box in 1994, reunited with rescuer Joe Campbell in 2016, calls him her ‘guardian angel’ 32 years later
articles.summary: UK News: A woman who was abandoned inside a phone box as a newborn has forged an extraordinary bond with the stranger who found and saved her more than three d.
articles.body: A woman who was abandoned inside a phone box as a newborn has forged an extraordinary bond with the stranger who found and saved her more than three decades ago. April Paul, now 32, considers her rescuer Joe Campbell part of her family, even as she comes to terms with the possibility that she may never understand why her birth mother left her.According to SWNS, April was found in a phone box on April 30, 1994, with her umbilical cord still attached. Joe Campbell, who was 30 at the time, discovered her after initially thinking he had spotted what looked like “a bag of chips”. He alerted the police, setting in motion the events that would eventually lead to April being adopted at the age of three.A reunion 22 years laterJoe was unable to maintain contact with April while she was growing up after being prevented from contacting her by social services. Despite this, he never forgot the baby he had found that day.In 2016, when April was 22, she launched an appeal to find the man who had rescued her. Joe recognised the story and came forward, allowing the pair to reconnect after 22 years.Their reunion has since developed into a relationship that April describes as being like gaining a family all over again.“Joe is complete family,” she said. “It’s like I was adopted again but in the right way this time around.”April has also grown close to Joe’s children, whom she now regards as her siblings. The pair see each other nearly every week and regularly stay at each other’s homes.“He never stopped thinking about me,” April said. “I don’t know what this man is – an angel.”April accepts she may never know why she was abandonedApril also tried to find her birth mother after reconnecting with Joe. She was able to visit her mother’s home in 2016 and have an initial conversation, but says there has been no contact since.Although she continues to have questions, April told Talk to the Press that she is beginning to accept that the answers she has wanted throughout her life may never come.“The truth is I absolutely do still want answers from my mum,” she said. “I think a part of me probably always will.”“I wish more than anything that I could understand why she left me and have the answers to questions I’ve carried around my whole life.”But April said the ongoing search has also become painful.“Realistically, I don’t think I’m ever going to get those answers from her,” she said. “Continuing to search and holding onto the hope that I might eventually get them is actually causing me more hurt.”Her daughter’s question left her searching for wordsApril, who works for a bank and lives in West London, said becoming a mother herself has made her childhood experiences particularly poignant.She recalled a conversation with her daughter, who asked her how she knew how to be a mother despite never having had one herself.“My daughter said to me the other day, ‘Mum, how do you know how to be a mum when you never had one?’”April told her daughter that being a mother was simply natural to her.But when her daughter asked, “Why couldn’t your mum be your mum?”, April could only respond: “I don’t know.”Joe continues to be there for AprilFor April, Joe is no longer simply the man who discovered her in a phone box. He has become someone she can rely on as family.“Joe saved my life 32 years ago, but he’s so much more than the man who found me,” she said.April recently recalled Joe turning up at her home despite having undergone knee surgery just three weeks earlier. His children had planned to visit April for dinner, but Joe arrived himself, despite still limping from the operation.“I said, ‘what are you doing here?’ Of course he brought me loads of shopping, gifts and perfume,” she said.According to April, that gesture was typical of Joe.“He’s the type of man you would call in the middle of the night and he would come straight away,” she said.April is now fundraising to help Joe retire early, hoping to give something back to the man whose decision to stop and investigate a seemingly abandoned “bag of chips” changed both their lives forever.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Vermont man guilty of attempted murder for shooting three Palestinians
articles.summary: The shooting in November 2023 came amid a rise in Islamophobia and antisemitism following the start of the Israel-Gaza war.
articles.body:
A man has been convicted of attempted murder for shooting three Palestinian university students in the US state of Vermont nearly three years ago, with the jury rejecting his insanity claims.

Lawyers for Jason Eaton, 51, said he believed he heard instructions from the CIA and Mossad over the radio to shoot someone before he attacked Hisham Awartani, Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid near the University of Vermont.

Eaton never denied being the shooter but pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. He now awaits sentencing, where he could be given life in prison.

The November 2023 attack left Awartani paralysed from the waist down, and wounded the two others.

The week-long trial included testimony from the three students, who are now all aged 23, and from psychiatrists called by both the defence and prosecution.

According to the Associated Press, Eaton stared blankly as the jury read the guilty verdict, while Awartani - who attended the trial in a wheelchair - and Aliahmad smiled and hugged those around them.

His defence team had argued Eaton's mental health had spiralled, pushing him into a bout of psychosis, after he lost his job at a credit union weeks before the incident.

Eaton's lawyers said he believed the CIA was talking to him through a local radio broadcast and directed him to "go out and shoot somebody".

"He believed he'd been instructed to do this by a government agency or God," defence attorney Joshua O'Hara said.

The shooting occurred the month after the start of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war and amid a rise in Islamophobia and antisemitism in the US.

It reportedly took place as the three men were walking near Eaton's home, speaking a mix of Arabic and English and wearing traditional Palestinian scarves known as keffiyehs.

Abdalhamid was a Haverford College student. Awartani attended Brown University in Rhode Island, and Ahmed was a student at Trinity College in Connecticut.

The three had previously attended school in Ramallah together and were visiting Awartani's grandmother for Thanksgiving.
